newsitem.title: UK: June non-OPEC supply down, Latin America up -IEA.
newsitem.headline: June non-OPEC supply down, Latin America up -IEA.

text.p: June oil supply from non-OPEC countries fell by 100,000 to 44.5 million barrels per day, mainly due to a decline in Russian exports, the International Energy Agency said on Tuesday.

Exports from the territories of the former Soviet Union fell by 200,000 bpd because of pipeline repairs and Black Sea port closures, but the loss was partly offset by gains in Latin America, the Paris-based agency said.

"Mexico and Argentina saw increased output, while in the OECD, higher volumes from Canada, the UK and Australia more than compensated for declines in the U.S. and Norway," the agency said in its latest monthly report.

The IEA said it was still projecting non-OPEC crude oil supply to be 47.2 mbpd in 1998, some 2.0 mpbd above this year's expected average, as new North Sea fields come on line and oil production recovers in the former Soviet Union.

Latin America produced 6.89 mpbd in June, some 45,000 bpd more than in the previous month, with Mexico leading he way thanks to rising flows of offshore Mayan crude and better natural gas liquid production, the IEA said.
"In addition, gains of 5-10,000 bpd are estimated to have taken place in Argentina, Colombia and Ecuador," the report said.
Mexican output is expected to rise steadily from the current 3.38 mbpd to 3.47 mbpd by fourth quarter 1997.

But potentially the largest increase in Latin America will come from Colombia where oil production is expected to increase by 147,000 bpd when two new production modules pump more Cusiana crude through the nearly completed Ocensa pipe.
"Most of the gains are expected by September, when output is projected at 760,000 bpd, up from the 640,000 bpd estimated for June," the IEA said.

But overall Colombian forecasts for 3Q 97 and 4Q 97 were cut by 50,000 and 70,000 bpd respectively, due to security problems which have pushed back the start of new production in the Cupiagaua field until 2Q 98, it added.

Brazilian output was also forecast to rise by the year's end as the offshore Campos Basin and Barracuda fields came on stream. Brazilian oil production was 880,000 bpd in March and was forecast to hit 1 mbpd by the end of 1997.

British oil output in June increased by 60 kbpd, to 2.51 mbpd, as off-shore loading fields produced more, while Norwegian supply dropped by 85 kbpd, to 3.25 mbpd, as planned maintenance ate into output from the Oseberg system.

Canadian production was 2.43 mbpd, up 100,000 bpd, as synthetic crude output returned to normal after heavy maintenance and there was a 40,000 bpd drop in U.S. supply to 8.65 mbpd. Lower Alaskan figures were blamed by the IEA.
The IEA stuck to its forecast that former Soviet Union oil production will increase by 200,000 bpd in 1998, reversing a ten-year pattern of decline.
But much of the recovery will occur outside Russia, in former Soviet territory.
"More than half of the 1998 rise is expected to occur in Azerbaijan following the start-up of the offshore Chirag oil field in late 1997," the IEA said.

Kazakhstan's production should rise 95,000 bpd this year and 45,000 next, while Russian crude oil production will increase by 50,000 bpd as a result of joint-venture output destined for overseas markets.
